title: Standing before art
hook: a painting you can stand before for five minutes, until it starts to look back

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sacred buildings, and your line was as a guest. A new week starts indoors, in front of one picture.

A museum gallery on a weekday afternoon. People drift past the paintings the way they drift past shop windows: a glance, a phone held up, the next frame. Then one person stops in front of a single canvas and doesn't move. A minute. Three. The guard glances over. She's still there. Something has happened between her and the picture that didn't happen for anyone walking by. Today: standing before one piece, long enough for it to change.
screen: `A GLANCE, A PHONE, THE NEXT FRAME.` → `ONE PERSON STOPS.` → `LONG ENOUGH FOR IT TO CHANGE.`

segments.voice: First, the artist as gifted. In the Book of Exodus, when the people build the tabernacle, the text names a craftsman, Bezalel. God filled him, it says, with the spirit of God, with wisdom and understanding and knowledge, and with skill in every kind of work: gold, silver, bronze, stone, wood. In that story, making beautiful things is itself a gift of the spirit. Second, the image. In the letter to the Colossians, Christ is called "the image of the invisible God." The Greek word for image there is eikon. In Orthodox churches, the painted holy images are called icons, and people stand and pray before them. Orthodox writers have described an icon not as an idol but as a window, a place where the eye rests while the heart goes further. Third, why five minutes. The first look takes in the subject: a face, a field, a bowl of fruit. The second look finds the colors. After a few minutes you begin to see choices: why that shadow, why that empty corner, why the light falls there and not here. The longer you stand, the more the picture seems to hold. Fourth, what standing does. Standing before something, rather than scrolling past it, is a posture of respect, the way people stand before a person they honor. You don't need to know art history. You only have to give one picture more time than it usually gets, and see what it gives back.
screen: `BEZALEL: FILLED WITH SKILL.` · `EIKON: THE IMAGE.` · `THE FIRST LOOK, THEN THE SECOND.` · `STANDING IS A KIND OF RESPECT.` · then, large: `THE IMAGE OF THE INVISIBLE GOD.`

segments.voice: Choose one artwork, a painting at home, an icon, a famous canvas on your screen, a child's drawing on the fridge, and look only at it. First the whole thing, then one corner, then the colors, then the light, where it comes from and where it lands; when your attention slips, go back to one detail. If you pray, let the looking be a prayer without words; if you don't, simply stand before it.
Eikon. The Greek word for image, behind the Christian icon: one painting, one icon, one drawing, looked at for longer than a glance, until it begins to give back. Today's word.
Your line: stand before it. Most pictures get a glance; one can get more. Day one thousand forty-four counts.

howItsDone: In Orthodox churches, people pray before icons, and visitors to museums and churches sometimes make a practice of slow looking: standing before one work for several minutes instead of passing many quickly.
